♻ ☆ Type-IV 't Hooft Anomalies on the Lattice: Emergent Higher-Categorical Symmetries and Applications to LSM Systems
Tsubasa Oishi, Hiromi Ebisu
't Hooft anomalies impose fundamental constraints on quantum matter and often lead to emergent symmetry structures upon gauging. We analyze a lattice model with four global symmetries realizing a mixed anomaly described by $\sim a_1\wedge a_2\wedge a_3\wedge a_4$, where the $a_i$ denote background gauge fields for the global symmetries. Through explicit lattice gauging, we demonstrate the emergence of higher symmetry structures, including 2-group, non-invertible, and higher fusion categorical symmetries. We also provide a field theoretical understanding of these results. Applying this framework to systems with Lieb-Schultz-Mattis anomalies, obtained by promoting part of the internal symmetries to translational symmetries, we demonstrate that modulated (dipole) symmetries and non-invertible translation symmetry arise as direct counterparts of those in systems with purely internal type-IV anomalies. Importantly, we uncover a qualitatively new feature absent in previously studied modulated symmetries and non-invertible translation: their realization can become intrinsically defect-dependent. In particular, the emergent symmetry structure changes depending on whether symmetry defects are present. This work establishes a concrete lattice realization of mixed anomalies and reveals a rich structure of emergent symmetries, thereby clarifying their role in constraining quantum phases of matter.

♻ ☆ Obstruction to local entropy laws on arbitrary black-hole cuts in five-dimensional Einstein--Gauss--Bonnet gravity
Cendikiawan Suryaatmadja, Robert B. Mann
We study local entropy laws on arbitrary cuts of event horizons in five-dimensional Einstein--Gauss--Bonnet gravity, treated as an exact theory. No covariant local entropy can both reproduce the stationary black-hole entropy and be nondecreasing between every ordered pair of cuts, provided its density is smooth on an invariant open set of off-shell metric and cut jets containing a flat planar cut and every cut used in the argument. No global bound on derivative order is assumed. The counterexamples to the second law are vacuum black holes perturbed by a gravitational wave, with a strongly hyperbolic formulation near the relevant horizon interval and its stationary future. Shear makes the intrinsic curvature of a cut depend on its bending. The stationary entropy fixes the coefficient of this curvature term, and local corrections cannot cancel its response to cut bending. The obstruction appears at second order in wave amplitude on a smooth horizon, without a merger or topology change.
♻ ☆ Fractal phase structure of QCD under imaginary rotation
Rin Takada
We show that in hot QCD rotating at an imaginary angular velocity $\tildeΩ_I$, the angular velocity selects not only the temperature of the bulk but whether charge conjugation $C$ is broken there. For QCD at temperature $T$ and imaginary quark chemical potential $θ$, with $\tildeΩ_I/2π=p/q$ in lowest terms, the bulk far from the rotation axis is in the same thermal equilibrium state as nonrotating QCD at temperature $T/q$ and imaginary quark chemical potential $θ'=qθ+π(p+q+1)$; this follows from the Euclidean boundary conditions and locality alone, and holds nonperturbatively whenever the equivalent nonrotating system has a finite correlation length. Consequently, even at zero quark chemical potential, the bulk is placed at the Roberge-Weiss (RW) point whenever $p$ and $q$ are both odd, and $C$ is spontaneously broken there for $T>qT_{\rm RW}$, with $T_{\rm RW}$ the RW endpoint temperature. The bulks at $\tildeΩ_I=2π/3$ and $4π/3$, for example, are both at temperature $T/3$, yet only the former can break $C$. The set of imaginary angular velocities at which $C$ is broken has a fractal structure: raising $T$ adds rationals of ever larger denominator. At irrational $\tildeΩ_I/2π$ the bulk corresponds to zero-temperature QCD at any $T$ and remains confined.

♻ ☆ IR/UV mixing from higher-order interactions in a Scalar Field
Satish Ramakrishna
The observed vacuum energy lies far below the usual quantum-field-theoretic estimate. We construct a preferred-frame reduced scalar Hamiltonian in which a nonlocal quartic field derivative interaction produces a wavevector dependence proportional to $|\vec k|^8$ for modes below a smoothly defined scale. Within the quartic oscillator regime, the ground-state energy and excitation gaps are $\propto |\vec k|^{8/3}$. The preferred frame is characterized by a timelike clock-field background. The Planck energy is reached at a substantially smaller value of the spatial wavevector due to its supra-linear mode-energy dependence. The proposed interaction is instantaneous in the preferred frame and yields a Hamiltonian bounded below. Normalizing the peak of the ground-state energy to the Planck scale, together with Cohen-Kaplan-Nelson (CKN) saturation, applied as a matching recipe rather than as an {\it {ab initio}} calculation, fixes the cutoff scale at $k_G\sim k_{Pl}^{1/3}k_{box}^{2/3}$. Modes above the smooth cutoff scale retain their ordinary scalar dynamics. We assume that the interaction-induced ground-state energy shift gravitates, as do other contributions. CKN saturation is imposed on the total vacuum energy, comprising this shift and the other vacuum contributions. Identifying the inferred infrared scale phenomenologically with the cosmic event horizon reproduces the holographic-dark-energy relation $ρ_{vac}\propto\frac{M_{Pl}^2}{R_h^2}$, provided the coupling tracks the horizon; the resulting holographic fluid has $w_0\simeq-0.89$.
♻ ☆ Localisation with on-shell supersymmetry algebras via the Batalin-Vilkovisky formalism: Localisation as gauge fixing
Leron Borsten, Dimitri Kanakaris, Hyungrok Kim
The Batalin-Vilkovisky formalism provides a powerful technique to deal with gauge and global (super)symmetries that may only hold on shell. We argue that, since global (super)symmetries and gauge symmetries appear on an equal footing in the Batalin-Vilkovisky formalism, similarly localisation with respect to global (super)symmetries appears on an equal footing with gauge fixing of gauge symmetries; in general, when the gauge-fixing condition is not invariant under the global symmetries, localisation (with respect to a localising fermion) and gauge fixing (with respect to a gauge-fixing fermion) combine into a single operation. Furthermore, this perspective enables supersymmetric localisation using only on-shell supermultiplets, dispensing with auxiliary fields, extending an insight first discovered by Losev and Lysov arXiv:2312.13999. We provide the first examples of on-shell localisation for quantum field theories (together with a companion paper by Arvanitakis arXiv:2511.00144).

We also tested the cleaning method in a high-voltage photogun, where QE showed the same initial increase and subsequent decline. ☆ Shift current as a stacking spectroscopy of hexagonal boron nitride multilayers

We test that assumption by computing the polarization and the shift-current tensor from first principles across the stacking landscape of bi-, tri-, and tetralayer hexagonal boron nitride. The two quantities share one robust property: the vertical response reverses with the polarization while the in-plane one does not. Beyond this rule, the correspondence must be read with caution: stackings with identical polarization carry vertical monochromatic photocurrents of opposite sign; the spectra reorganize and even reverse sign at some photon energies along a constant-polarization plateau; and the strongest vertical peak of the entire pathway sits where the polarization crosses zero. The reason is structural: the polarization counts polar interfaces, while the shift current reads their positions. Broadband illumination reads the domain sign; monochromatic photocurrent maps can read the stacking registry. In a sliding ferroelectric, the bulk photovoltaic effect can operate as a stacking spectroscopy.

Kagome lattices provide an exciting space for the exploration of graphene-like $π$-conjugated molecular systems with flat bands. Using heterotriangulene-derived precursors, along with an on-surface Ullmann coupling process, makes growing polymers with Kagome lattices accessible and straightforward. Here, we use scanning tunneling microscopy alongside high-resolution atomic force microscopy to examine the evolution of tribromotrioxaazatriangulene on Au(111) into ordered, covalent films. Using density functional theory and scanning probe methods, we find previously unreported organometallic intermediate states involving Au adatoms incorporated within the growing polymer lattice. We also find that a majority of polymer edges remain brominated up to 250 $^{\circ}$C and a large number of edges bonded to Au adatoms coordinated to an adjacent bromine atom. These observations suggest that residual bromine could play a role in stabilizing the polymer edges to Au adatoms and thereby influence the growth pathways that lead to ordered Kagome polymer lattices.

♻ ☆ SPARC: Evidence-guided adaptive model composition for materials discovery
Sissi Feng, Yuchen Han, Runze Zhang, Jiaru Bai, Yixi Li, Brandon Sutherland, Ali Shayesteh Zeraati, Jason Hattrick-Simpers, Varinia Bernales, Alán Aspuru-Guzik, Yang Bai
Closed-loop experimentation requires more than selecting the next experiment. It must also determine which existing measurements and model-derived relationships are sufficiently supported to influence that decision. Here we introduce SPARC (Sparse Predictive Aggregation of Regression Components), a framework that continually revises this support as experimental evidence accumulates. Competing model families are evaluated through out-of-fold predictions, so that each model is tested on observations not used in its corresponding fit. Sparse posterior composition assigns model influence according to predictive contributions supported by the out-of-fold evidence, retaining complementary contributions from several model families. Candidate-dependent predictive dispersion and residual variability define trust, which modulates exploration alongside the predicted response. Independent diagnostics also prioritize existing measurements for prospective verification, with model-derived trust reported alongside them. Across eight published materials datasets, SPARC achieved higher $R^2$ than the corresponding literature-reported values in six, with relative gains of up to 77% without the density-functional-theory- or experiment-derived descriptors used by several published pipelines. In an automated alkaline oxygen-evolution-reaction campaign, 8 of 11 SPARC-selected experiments reached overpotentials below 300 mV, with a best value of 242 mV, compared with 18 of 125 initial experiments. Measurements prioritized for verification before repetition subsequently deviated by 76 mV on average, compared with 27 mV for matched controls. SPARC therefore turns experimental evidence into a basis for revising model influence, directing exploration and identifying measurements that warrant verification.

♻ ☆ Frame Based Inelasticity for Fracture in Anisotropic Media
Robert Lipton, Prakash K. C.
A field theory is presented for predicting damage and fracture in brittle materials. Four concepts are used: a new nonlocal deformation gradient for dynamic stress analysis in anisotropic media, a new type of phase field coming from a constitutive law, the evolution of material displacement from Newton's second law, and a new incorporation of scaled strength surfaces into constitutive laws for predicting dynamic and quasi-static fracture patterns. The elastic softening is governed by the strain dynamics through the constitutive law and in this way we provide the two way coupling between strain and fracture. Simulations validating the approach for both dynamic and quasi-static fracture analysis are compared to experimental results and other simulation methods. The model is capable of predicting material strength in titania and the competition between strength and energy in soda lime glass and titana and captures dynamic crack branching in soda lime glass and concrete.

♻ ☆ Origin and photoluminescence of a shallow hydrogen-related donor in silicon
Miaomiao Han, Peter Deak, Bing Huang, Adam Gali
Paramagnetic color centers in silicon are being investigated recently for use in quantum technologies. While the origin of most of the prominent photoluminescence (PL) lines are well understood, that is not the case for those connected to hydrogen, even though it is almost always present in silicon, e.g., shallow hydrogen-related donors (SHDs), but their atomic structure remains elusive. Recent experiments suggested connection between the SHDs and the so-called X and the B$_i$ (or X$_i$) PL-lines. An SHD, termed the MT2 center, was tentatively assigned to a bistable, negative-U defect, arising due to the interaction of hydrogen with the self-interstitial complex I$_4$. Using high-level density functional theory calculations, we investigate the interaction of hydrogen with self-interstitial complexes In. A shallow effective-mass-theory donor arises when hydrogen attacks a Si-Si bond in I$_n$, inserting itself as a bond-center interstitial (I$_n$H$_{BC}$) in an exothermic reaction. We demonstrate this in the case of a single self-interstitial and of a complex of four. The latter I$_\mathrm{4}$H$_\mathrm{BC}$ complex shows electronic, spin and PL properties remarkably close to MT2. We find that hydrogen in the presence of I$_4$ follows the same behavior as in pristine silicon, i.e., it is a negative-U bistable defect, only detectable under illumination. In the I$_4$H$_{BC}$ complex, H can hop via photo-assisted mechanism between equivalent BC sites of the I$_4$ complex, leading to a motional averaged tetragonal symmetry as experimentally observed for MT2. The zero-phonon line is distinct from the X-line (attributed to the bare I$_4$ complex), and falls well into the range of the X$_i$ lines. Our results identify the I$_4$H complex as a prototype for a class of SHDs, inferring that similar SHDs may arise, with the X$_i$ lines as their PL fingerprints, when H attacks I$_n$ clusters.
♻ ☆ Two Unconventional Hall Effects in the Kagome Magnet TmMn4Cr$_2$Sn$_6$
Mohamed El Gazzah, Fehmi Sami Yasin, Bishal Thapa, Sk Jamaluddin, Daniel Lu, Abhijeet Nayak, Resham Babu Regmi, Mary Katherine Carroll, Igor I. Mazin, Nirmal J. Ghimire
We identify two Hall anomalies in the kagome magnet TmMn$_4$Cr$_2$Sn$_6$. We propose that the high-field anomaly reflects a discontinuous spin reorientation and differing sublattice contributions to Hall transport and magnetization. At low fields, Hall hysteresis persists despite negligible magnetic hysteresis, suggesting a chirality-related contribution, although its microscopic origin remains unresolved. These contrasting regimes show how magnetic transitions can mimic unconventional Hall signals and highlight the limits of magnetization-based Hall decomposition.
♻ ☆ Double quantum spin Hall phase in bilayer ZrTe$_5$
Chao Chen Ye, Gábor Kalla, Marcio Costa, Jianting Ye, Jagoda Sławińska
Quantum spin Hall (QSH) insulators host helical edge states that enable dissipationless transport, but realizing multiple conducting channels in experimentally accessible materials with large band gaps remains challenging. Here, we show that AB-stacked untwisted bilayer ZrTe$_5$ naturally realizes a double QSH phase in its energetically most stable structure, revealing an unexpected multichannel transport regime. The phase hosts two pairs of helical edge states and a doubled quantized spin Hall conductivity, with spin Chern number $C_s=2$ despite the conventional $\mathbb{Z}_2=0$ classification. Lattice deformation tunes the system through a metallic state to a conventional QSH phase with $\mathbb{Z}_2=1$, enabling control of the number of helical channels. Remarkably, the quantized spin Hall response persists over an energy window substantially larger than the bulk band gap, exceeding 100~meV. Our results establish bilayer ZrTe$_5$ as an experimentally accessible multichannel QSH system in which interlayer coupling and lattice deformation control topological edge transport.

♻ ☆ What Photocurrent Versus Effective Voltage Tells Us About Charge Generation in Organic Solar Cells
Ardalan Armin, Austin M. Kay, Drew B. Riley, Oskar J. Sandberg, Paul Meredith
The photocurrent of an organic solar cell is routinely plotted against an effective voltage and used to extract an exciton dissociation probability, and through it a free-charge generation efficiency. The photocurrent measures neither. Using a drift-diffusion model in which free-charge generation is field independent and losses occur only by bimolecular recombination, we show that the apparent dissociation probability returned by this procedure lies well below unity even for complete dissociation. Across wide variations of carrier mobility and recombination strength it is a single-valued function of the fill factor and coincides with the short-circuit charge collection efficiency, reporting neither the generation yield nor anything about collection beyond what the fill factor already shows. Even for ideal transport the normalised photocurrent saturates below unity at an intensity-independent first-order limit set by recombination of photogenerated carriers with injected equilibrium charge. Applied to four organic solar cells whose generation efficiencies are known independently, the apparent dissociation probabilities track the short-circuit collection efficiency rather than the generation yield. We therefore suggest this construction not be used, particularly in the high-efficiency non-fullerene acceptor systems that are now state of the art.
♻ ☆ Facile On-Chip Growth and Spatially Selective Color Tuning of CsPbBr$_{3}$@TFA Nanoplatelets via Ion Engineering
Sana Khan, Saeed Goudarzi, Lars Sonneveld, Felix Thiel, Stephan Schäffer, Bart Macco, Ke Ran, Sercan Ozen, Naho Kurahashi, Peter Haring Bolívar, Felix Lang, Bruno Ehrler, Burkay Uzlu, Thomas Riedl, Gerhard Müller-Newen, Surendra. B. Anantharaman, Maryam Mohammadi, Max. C. Lemme
Metal halide perovskite (MHP) nanoplatelets are attractive for integrated optoelectronics because of their strong light-matter interactions and composition-tunable optical response. However, their high surface-to-volume ratio promotes surface defects and trap-assisted nonradiative recombination. In addition, their ionic nature facilitates rapid halide migration and limits selective composition tuning. Here, we combine in-synthesis (in situ) and post-synthesis ion engineering to suppress nonradiative recombination and enable selective on-chip color conversion. CsPbBr$_{3}$ nanoplatelets were grown directly on-chip via a solution process incorporating trifluoroacetate (TFA$^{-}$) pseudohalides. CsPbBr$_{3}$@TFA emits at 520 nm with a linewidth of 14.56 $\% \pm$ 0.5 nm and an average lifetime of 26.38 ns. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy shows that TFA$^{-}$ passivates uncoordinated Pb$^{2+}$ and suppresses metallic lead (Pb$^{0}$) formation. Spatially selective halide exchange was then achieved using a photolithographically patterned PMMA/Al$_{2}$O$_{3}$ mask to confine HCl vapor exposure. In the unmasked regions, the photoluminescence peak shifts from 520 nm to 413 nm, producing laterally defined green- and violet-emitting regions. The nanoplatelets were further integrated with graphene field-effect transistors, yielding responsivities of 2.5 x 10$^{5}$ A W$^{-1}$ at 450 nm and 1.9 x 10$^{5}$ A W$^{-1}$ at 370 nm, respectively. Our method enables scalable growth and selective color tuning of MHP nanoplatelets for on-chip optoelectronic integration.

♻ ☆ Maximum-Temperature Theorem for Nanothermometry
Taras Plakhotnik
We derive a sharp upper bound on the quasi-steady temperature rise of a sensor of arbitrary shape and known thermometric volume $V_\mathrm{s}$, placed anywhere inside a region enclosed by an isothermal reference surface. The bound also requires the maximum net heat power $\dot Q_{\scriptscriptstyle \mathcal S \subseteq \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm r}}^{\max}$ crossing any closed surface within the region and a lower bound on its thermal conductivity $κ_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm r}}}$. It is otherwise independent of the heat-source distribution, domain shape, and source-ensor distance. For $\dot Q_{\scriptscriptstyle \mathcal S \subseteq \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm r}}^{\max}=50~\mathrm{pW}$, $κ_{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm r}}} =0.1~\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $V_{\mathrm s}$ equal to the volume of a $60~\mathrm{nm}$-diameter sphere, the theorem permits a maximum temperature rise of approximately $2~\mathrm{mK}$. Neither source localization nor uncertain source--sensor separation can therefore account for reported kelvin-scale intracellular readings under steady-state heat conduction. The result applies to sensors based on nanodiamonds, upconversion nanoparticles, fluorescent polymer beads, and core-shell quantum dots.

♻ ☆ Digital-Alloy Bragg Mirrors in High-Q Microcavities for Polariton Lasing
V. A. Stolyarov, A. S. Kurdyubov, A. V. Trifonov, M. Yu. Petrov, I. V. Ignatiev, V. A. Lovtcius, S. A. Eliseev, Yu. P. Efimov, M. S. Lozhkin, A. V. Kavokin
We present an approach to the molecular beam epitaxy of high-$Q$ planar GaAs-based microcavities in which the AlGaAs high-index layers of the distributed Bragg reflectors are replaced by short-period GaAs/AlAs superlattices (digital alloys) engineered to provide the same effective Al content. This design enables a significant reduction of interface roughness, precise control of both the $λ/4$ optical thickness and the effective Al content, suppression of the propagation of certain structural defects, and efficient tuning of the intrinsic absorption at the polariton emission wavelength through optimization of the superlattice parameters. Using this approach, we have grown a microcavity with a low polariton lasing threshold of $P_{\mathrm{th}} \approx (570 \pm 90)$ W/cm$^2$ and a high experimental quality factor of $Q_{\mathrm{expt}} \approx (5.4 \pm 0.1) \times 10^4$. This value exceeds by a factor of 2 the theoretical estimate obtained within a model in which the digital alloy is replaced by a ternary AlGaAs alloy with the same effective Al content. We demonstrate that accurate modeling of the stop-band characteristics and the $Q$ factor requires incorporation of the modified electronic density of states in the superlattice, including quantum-confinement and excitonic effects.

♻ ☆ Chiral Spinterfaces as an Overlooked Component of the Chiral-Induced Spin Selectivity Effect
Franziska Schölzel, Aybüke Gülkaya, Rico Ehrler, Dominik Hornig, Lokesh Rasabathina, Aleksandra Lindner, Jürgen Lindner, Aleksandr Kazimir, Christina Lamers, Dietrich R. T. Zahn, Michael Mehring, Olav Hellwig, Shuxia Tao, Georgeta Salvan
The chiral-induced spin selectivity (CISS) effect is commonly associated with spin-selective transport through chiral molecules, while the role of molecule-electrode interfaces remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that adsorption of chiral amino acid derived molecules on ferromagnetic Ni films with native NiO layer induces a remanent chirality-dependent magneto-optical response. Systematic control experiments establish that this response originates from the molecule-NiO/Ni interface, rather than the molecular layer or bulk ferromagnet. First-principles calculations reveal preferential carboxylate binding and interfacial charge redistribution extending into the NiO surface layers, demonstrating how molecular adsorption modifies the electronic structure of the oxide. Together, these results provide evidence for the formation of chiral spinterfaces, where molecular chirality and interfacial electronic structure give rise to a distinct magnetic response. Our findings highlight the previously overlooked role of molecule-electrode interfaces in CISS-related systems and identify interfacial electronic and magnetic properties as important considerations for understanding and controlling spin selectivity.

♻ ☆ AutoDFT: A Closed-Loop Multi-Agent Framework for Autonomous DFT Calculations KDD 2027
Penghui Yang, Zhonghan Zhang, Yue Li, Xinrun Wang, Yanchen Deng, Yuhao Lu, Bijun Tang, Zheng Liu, Bo An
Density functional theory (DFT) serves as the basis for computational discovery in materials science and chemistry, yet each calculation demands extensive human effort: adjusting algorithms when convergence stalls, revising plans when unexpected physics emerges, and inserting steps as intermediate results reshape the problem. Existing LLM-based agents automate only the initial planning stage, producing a full execution plan upfront and leaving all subsequent adaptation to hand-crafted rules. As a result, these workflows remain fragile, do not generalize well beyond pre-planned scenarios, and often require expert intervention when failures or unexpected intermediate results require changes to the calculation path. Here, we introduce AutoDFT, a closed-loop multi-agent framework that embeds LLM reasoning into every stage of the DFT lifecycle, where a strategic planner produces a skeletal plan of step objectives; a step planner generates numerical parameters just in time from preceding results; and a monitor-recover-reflect cycle diagnoses failures, repairs them, and revises the plan when the evidence justifies it. We demonstrate both breadth and depth: breadth on VASPBench, a purpose-built benchmark spanning 34 tasks and 9 DFT calculation types, where AutoDFT achieves 94.1% task-level success with GPT-5.2; and depth on established materials databases, where AutoDFT produces quantitatively reliable property predictions across electronic, magnetic, and energetic properties. By closing the loop between planning and execution, AutoDFT enables experimentalists without deep computational expertise to obtain reliable first-principles results. Our code is available at https://github.com/penghui-yang/AutoDFT.

♻ ☆ Fitting the topology of synthetic particle systems with a novel graph representation
Martin Alexander Memmesheimer, Claudia Redenbach
The shape and arrangement of particles in a material determine its macroscopic properties. The generation of synthetic data with varying particle structure, often represented as 3D voxel images, combined with simulation of macroscopic properties reveals structure-property relations. Most particle generation models focus on single-particle characteristics like shape and size. We aim at fitting the topology of the particle system using tools from persistent homology. However, the large size of the required 3D image data makes existing methods computationally infeasible. We bridge this gap by introducing a novel graph representation of particle systems and transferring the computation of persistent homology from the image domain to the graph domain. This yields a postprocessing method for synthetic images of particle systems, that is independent of the underlying generation method and improves topological and geometrical agreement with real particle systems while preserving morphological characteristics such as the particle size distribution.

♻ ☆ A unified geometric design framework for kirigami structures
Qinghai Jiang, Gary P. T. Choi
Kirigami turns a thin sheet with cuts into a shape-morphing mechanical metamaterial, with applications across science and engineering. While various two- and three-dimensional kirigami design methods have been developed, most of them are only applicable to a limited class of kirigami structures. In this work, we present a unified geometric design framework for kirigami structures. Since the states of a kirigami pattern differ only in which tile corners coincide, one tessellation routine generates them all, and edge-length equalities couple them. A single constrained optimization then designs 2D-to-2D, 2D-to-3D, and 3D-to-3D shape-morphing, compact reconfigurable, and rigidly deployable structures, and one sheet that deploys into two prescribed shapes. The designs further reveal geometric laws hidden in the kirigami mechanism, which explain how reconfiguration transposes the shape of a sheet, how one sheet bends into both a bowl and a saddle, and why the outline of a flat sheet limits the curvature it can reach when it closes again. Altogether, our work paves a new way for the design of shape-morphing mechanical metamaterials.
♻ ☆ Local moment magnon spectrum in conduction electron tunnelling
Peter Thalmeier, Alireza Akbari
The surface tunnelling spectrum of a dual system consisting of localised moments with antiferromagnetic order coupled to conduction electrons by on-site exchange interaction is investigated. In the static approximation of the local moment order it is known that magnetic band reconstruction leads to an anomalous tunnelling spectrum at the magnetic ordering vector of local moments although the latter cannot contribute directly. In this work we consider dynamic effects by including the scattering of conduction electrons from the local moment magnon excitations. They lead to self energies and renormalisation of conduction states which in turn appreciably modify the tunnelling spectrum beyond the influence of static order, interpreted as the appearance of magnon sidebands.

♻ ☆ Agentic programs: an emerging form of scientific software in computational materials science
Yunsung Lim, Haekwan Jeon, Jaesun Kim, Jisu Kim, Seungwu Han
Computational materials science has traditionally delegated algorithmic tasks to computers while leaving scientific judgments to humans. In this Perspective, we argue that agent harnesses built on large language models (LLMs) enable an emerging form of scientific software, agentic programs, integrating deterministic algorithms with bounded LLM-based judgment, task-specific verification, episodic maturation, and complete delegation. We illustrate these characteristics through DeMARS, which constructs atomistic models from experimentally measured disordered crystal structures.

♻ ☆ Probing Plasmonic Oscillations in 2D Moir'e Nanocrystal Superlattices by Low-Loss EELS
Swarnendu Das, Shengsong Yang, Kevin N. Moser, Marc R. Bourgeois, Quentin M. Ramasse, David J. Masiello, Christopher B. Murray, Eric A. Stach
Electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) has been established as a powerful analytical technique for investigating the oxidation state, band structure, and dielectric properties of materials with exceptional spatial resolution. Inspired by twisted 2D materials, we utilize low-loss EELS to examine the plasmonic excitations in 2D moiré Au nanocrystal superlattices (NCSLs) formed by liquid-air interface self-assembly using a double-dipping method. This approach produces stacked hexagonal layers that can be twisted, forming moiré patterns in NCSLs whose twist angles are precisely measured via scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM). Low-loss EELS effectively mitigates challenges arising from fabrication-induced non-uniformity and reveals a blue shift in plasmonic excitation when comparing single-layer, double-layer, and twisted configurations. This sharply contrasts with the optical spectroscopy measurements, which show an overall red shift relative to the EELS data. The high spatial resolution of STEM-EELS further demonstrates that twist-induced symmetry breaking strongly influences plasmonic behavior. Coupled dipole modeling explains the observed discrepancies: the electron beam excites out-of-plane polarization modes unavailable to optical probes, while optical measurements average over ensembles. Our findings highlight that EELS provides complementary information to optical spectroscopy for understanding how structural arrangements at the nanoscale influence collective electronic properties, advancing the design of plasmonic metamaterials.
♻ ☆ Equivariant Deep Learning in Direct-Product Space for Electronic-Structure Hamiltonian Prediction
Shi Yin, Zujian Dai, Xinyang Pan, Lixin He
Most existing equivariant architectures for Hamiltonian prediction propagate features in direct-sum spaces of irreducible spherical tensors, whereas the target Hamiltonian is naturally an operator block in a direct-product representation over local orbital and spin bases. This representation mismatch fragments contiguous Hamiltonian blocks, obscures direct manipulation of orbital couplings, and organizes features into irregular angular-momentum components that require numerous transformations and are poorly aligned with efficient hardware execution and memory management. To address both the representation mismatch and computational bottleneck, we propose DP-Learner, an equivariant learning framework that performs message passing directly on Hamiltonian-like operator blocks in the direct-product space. Theoretically, we propose Lie-generator-based directional embedding and invariantly weighted left--right products and contractions that preserve equivariance to SO(3), SU(2), and spatial inversions, without explicit Clebsch--Gordan decomposition or inverse reconstruction. Methodologically, we instantiate this principle as a Transformer architecture, in which Hamiltonian-like feature matrices or tensors evolve through equivariant operators in the direct-product space, while non-linear invariant scalar routing controls structured gating over matrix units, directional propagation, attention, and environment-embedded context interactions. We further construct MP-HAM-110K, a large-scale Hamiltonian dataset comprising more than 110,000 material structures covering 68 elements with both Hamiltonian and wavefunction data. Experiments on MP-HAM-110K and Materials-HAM-SOC demonstrate that DP-Learner dramatically improves Hamiltonian prediction accuracy and inference efficiency over the state-of-the-art method.
♻ ☆ Rippled graphene pores as fluidic memristive devices with synaptic and neuromorphic functionalities
Wenzhe Zhou, Dongjiao Ge, Ao Zhang, Jincheng Xu, Yu Ji, Yiran Gong, Wenchang Zhang, Jidong Li, Li Lin, Zhiping Xu, Pengzhan Sun
Nanofluidic memristive devices work with nanoscale pores and ions dissolved in water, which harness the ionic memory effect aiming to store and process information. These devices share the same charge carriers as biological systems and bring hope for better emulating the neural functions and developing ionic circuits for neuromorphic applications. Specially, theory and experiments suggest that nanoconfinement is essential for inducing a memory effect, which places limit on the pore size to nm-scale or smaller. Such devices are difficult to scale up with precision and operate with long-term stability. Here, we show that a micrometer size pore, generally expected to exhibit a linear ion transport, can display a pronounced memory effect, if its rim is wrapped by strongly curved and tightly stacked graphene. We attribute the observation to slow ion dynamics confined in the rippled graphene edges. The devices are easy to scale up and integrate into fluidic circuits. The memory effect is ion-selective and exhibits long endurance comparable to the lifetime of synaptic proteins, which enables reversible modification of the conductance states using programmable voltage spikes and various electrolytes over a long time, akin to biological synaptic plasticity. Thanks to this plasticity, our devices and their integrated circuits enable storing, transmitting and processing information with high reliability, fidelity and accuracy, as evidenced in the identification of both greyscale and color images, and in the real-time analysis of emulated neural signals. Our results highlight nanoscale morphology of the pore wall as an important parameter regulating ion transport and indicate that the stringent nanoconfinement for ionic memory can be lifted from restricting the pore size to designing its rim structure. The devices and their integrated circuits may find use in ionic neuromorphic applications.
♻ ☆ I$_4$ complex acting as near-infrared emitter with a quantum memory in silicon
Miaomiao Han, Song Li, Gergő Thiering, Thomas Frauenheim, Peter Deák, Bing Huang, Adam Gali

Using hybrid-functional (HSE06) density functional theory, we unambiguously establish the bare I$_4$ complex as the origin of the X-line: our calculations quantitatively reproduce the zero-phonon line, the complete phonon sideband structure---identifying the prominent secondary peaks as one- and two-phonon replicas of strongly coupled quasi-local modes---and the EPR hyperfine constants. The charge transition level is found at VBM$+$0.08~eV, conclusively ruling out the previously proposed association with the B3 EPR center and its correlated deep donor level. Most significantly, we identify a metastable spin-1 triplet excited state separated from the singlet by $\sim$1.6~meV, consistent with the NL51 EPR signal. The $D_{2d}$ symmetry of the defect suppresses intersystem crossing and phosphorescence by first-order spin--orbit coupling, implying an exceptionally long spin--lattice relaxation time. Combined with a spectrally resolvable zero-field splitting and near-infrared emission, the triplet state of the I$_4$ complex constitutes a viable spin quantum memory intrinsic to silicon.
♻ ☆ X-ray spectroscopic responses to magnetoelastic symmetry breaking in altermagnets
N. Sasabe, H. Koizumi, Y. Ishii, Y. Yamasaki
The multipole description of x-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), established through the sum rules of x-ray dichroism, provides a framework to describe magnetic and orbital responses in terms of ferroic multipole order parameters. X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) is known to probe spin, orbital, and anisotropic magnetic dipole moments. Its applications to altermagnets and noncollinear antiferromagnets have revealed that the XMCD response is often governed by the ferroic component of the photoexcited electronic states. In this work, we apply the multipole-based analysis of x-ray magnetic linear dichroism (XMLD) to altermagnets and demonstrate that XMLD response in altermagnets can be understood as a manifestation of magnetoelastic couplings between magnetic dipole and electric quadrupole moments. We show that the ferroic ordering of higher-rank magnetic multipoles, particularly spinful magnetic octupoles, gives rise to characteristic field-odd XMLD responses that directly reflect the underlying piezomagnetic response tensors allowed by magnetic point-group symmetry. Furthermore, we discuss XMCD responses induced by piezomagnetic effects, in which strain generates magnetic dipole moments. Our results establish XMLD and XMCD responses as element-specific probes of magnetoelastic multipole order in altermagnets and provide a general symmetry-based pathway to identify hidden ferroic multipoles and strain-controllable spin phenomena beyond conventional ferromagnetism.
♻ ☆ Competing redox and material redistribution during electrode ageing
Xiao Zhao, Yuchen Cao, Evan Z Carlson, Angel Burgos, Daniel Jacobs, Hanfeng Zhong, Lily Taylor, Haozhi Sha, Feng-yang Chen, Yu Shan, Hendrik Ohldag, Alexander Ditter, José A. Rodriguez, David Shapiro, William Chueh, Jianwei Miao
Electrochemical processes can involve coupled redox reactions, active-material redistribution and morphological evolution at buried electrode-electrolyte interfaces1-3. Operando imaging has revealed nanoscale heterogeneity in these processes3-9, but how reversible redox and cumulative material redistribution interact during cycles to govern electrode ageing remains unclear. Here we develop fast operando soft X-ray spectro-ptychography to track oxidation state, morphology and iron redistribution in the same nanoscale region of an alkaline iron anode over 20 h of cycling. We distinguish two coexisting processes operating on different timescales. Within each cycle, iron undergoes rapid, reversible conversion between metallic iron and iron oxyhydroxide (FeOOH) with little net iron redistribution. Across cycles, slower iron redistribution, consistent with dissolution and redeposition, promotes FeOOH-rich particle growth. Particle-resolved trajectories reveal that reversible conversion and iron accumulation coexist within individual particles, while particles with similar apparent growth exhibit markedly different changes in iron content. Local capacity initially increases as particles grow, then declines as more iron remains oxidized after charging and the reversible redox swing narrows. These findings suggest that cumulative Fe redistribution competes with reversible redox by progressively limiting the Fe available for charge storage. More generally, electrode ageing can begin during nearly reversible cycling, before capacity loss becomes apparent.
♻ ☆ Evaluating LLM-based AI agents integrated with materials synthesis tools: the case of atomic layer deposition
Angel Yanguas-Gil
This work provides an overview of the different strategies that can be used to evaluate the performance of AI models and agents based on large language models (LLMs) for materials synthesis. After providing a brief overview of the key technologies behind the current generation of AI agents based on LLMs, we summarize the different approaches to evaluating these models in the context of materials science and in particular on materials synthesis, with a specific emphasis on scenarios in which the models are directly integrated with experimental tools. We discuss evaluation strategies spanning knowledge and reasoning benchmarks, tool-use benchmarks, and closed loop benchmarks involving the interaction with experimental systems or realistic virtual tools. We use atomic layer deposition (ALD) as a case study, emphasizing how existing approaches in the literature both build from general approaches used beyond materials science and can be generalized to other materials synthesis techniques. Finally, we provide a practical evaluation framework to evaluate LLMs in the context of materials synthesis

☆ Quantum Many-Body Scars from Operator Size
Debarghya Chakraborty, Dario Rosa
We present a general construction of approximate many-body scar states in two copies of a system using a bilocal size interaction that couples one site to its partner on the other copy. For an uncoupled two-sided Hamiltonian whose terms have fixed size in an operator basis, we identify polynomially many Krylov basis states that it annihilates and that, in the thermodynamic limit, become concentrated on a single size sector. The size operator splits them into a tower of equally spaced levels that gives rise to coherent revivals characterized by collective oscillations of energy across the two copies. We provide a concrete realization of this construction in two copies of a general $q$-body nearest-neighbor spin chain, and the SYK model.

☆ Thermopower overshoot from collinear scattering in two-dimensional Fermi liquids
Johannes Hofmann
Electron transport is typically described in terms of relaxation times, which measure how quickly Fermi-surface deformations decay. We show here that the thermopower of a two-dimensional Fermi liquid instead probes the structure of these deformations in the form of their local temperature change, which we call the thermal dressing. This structure leads to an overshoot of the thermopower over its hydrodynamic value $- s/(ne)$ with increasing wave vector, before it falls to half that value in the ballistic limit. At low temperatures, the excess thermopower does not have the linear-in-temperature scaling expected of a Fermi liquid, but decreases only logarithmically as $1/\ln(T_F/T)$ at optimal wave vector. The overshoot is caused by collinear scattering, which redistributes energy over the Fermi surface and induces the thermal dressing, the strength of which grows with the angular harmonic index $m$ of the deformation. In contrast to tomographic effects in the charge conductivity, this overshoot does not rely on an odd-even effect in quasiparticle lifetimes and defines a distinct thermographic transport regime. The thermopower overshoot survives realistic disorder and should be detectable in a thermocouple with high-mobility samples.
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures
☆ Structure and relaxation of long-lived odd-parity modes in two-dimensional Fermi liquids
Stan Boeve, Johannes Hofmann
In two-dimensional Fermi liquids, odd-parity deformations of the Fermi surface relax anomalously slowly at a rate $\sim T^4$, where $T$ is the temperature. However, the leading-logarithmic prediction for the magnitude of this rate $\sim m^4 \ln m$, where $m$ is an angular harmonic index, exceeds exact-diagonalization results and the $\ln m$ scaling is not observed. We resolve this discrepancy by evaluating the 2D Fermi-liquid collision integral for general regular isotropic potentials to leading order in $T/T_F$, including the nonlogarithmic term beyond the $\ln(T_F/T)$ term. We find that the local temperature modulation of the odd mode, which we call the thermal dressing, suppresses relaxation by collinear scattering, with residual relaxation set by large-angle scattering. Such large-angle processes give corrections of order $\ln m/\ln(T_F/T)$ that are not small and must be resummed. We benchmark our results against exact-diagonalization calculations for constant interactions and find agreement over a range $m^2 T/T_F \lesssim 0.4$, and we provide closed-form results for the slowest odd-mode relaxation rate of a spin-polarized dipolar gas.
comment: 24 pages, 7 figures
☆ Optimised 8th-Order Trotter-Suzuki Schemes for Quantum Simulation
Marko Maležič, Johann Ostmeyer
Simulating quantum dynamics in many-body systems is one of the most promising applications of quantum computers. Product formulas are a natural choice for this task, since they map directly onto quantum gates, and increasing their order $n$ could lead to reduced gate depths, provided the parameters are chosen efficiently. So far, schemes beyond $6^{\textrm{th}}$ order have only been built as compositions of second-order schemes, while more general product formulas are known only up to $6^{\textrm{th}}$ order. In this work, we extend our optimisation framework to order $n = 8$, and find both more efficient compositions and the first $8^{\textrm{th}}$ order general schemes. Our formulas improve on the theoretical efficiency of the state-of-the-art schemes by Morales et al and we recommend two schemes explicitly. In simulations of the Heisenberg XZ chain one of our recommended schemes always outperforms those by Morales et al, though it is not always the same scheme that performs best. More generally, we observe that for Hamiltonians split into many non-commuting operators the uniformity of a Trotter decomposition becomes the main indicator of a scheme's performance. To assess the schemes' use on quantum hardware, we simulate noisy circuits with our new Qiskit plugin qiskit-omelyan. At current noise levels, the Leapfrog scheme remains the best choice, but as noise rates decrease toward fault tolerance, our recommended schemes become competitive.

☆ Magnetic-Field Response of a Hyperbolic Kitaev Spin Liquid
Tao Yang, Baigeng Wang, Rui Wang, Z. Y. Xie
Hyperbolic geometry can give rise to Kitaev spin liquids with distinct flux structures and Majorana spectra, raising the question of how these fractionalized states respond beyond exactly solvable limits. We address this question on the Kekulé-colored hyperbolic {8,3} lattice by developing an infinite projected entangled-pair-state approach with flux-resolved loop-gas initialization and geometry-adapted tensor-network contraction. Under uniform and staggered [111] magnetic fields, we find markedly different many-body responses. The uniform field induces a sharp change between competing variational branches at weak field, whereas the polarization and mean plaquette flux evolve over a much broader field range under the staggered field. Exchange-energy competition helps explain the different response scales, while third-order effective Majorana models in a fixed-flux background exhibit contrasting low-energy spectra. Our results connect the geometry-dependent fractionalized structure of a solvable hyperbolic spin liquid to its many-body response under physical perturbations that break flux conservation.

☆ Solving fermionic sign problems with physics-informed kernels
Kenji Fukushima, Friederike Ihssen, Renzo Kapust, Jan M. Pawlowski
We extend the generative sampling approach with physics-informed kernels (PIKs) [1,2] to a general class of physics systems with complex distributions and a structure also encountered in fermionic systems. The resolution of sign problems of generic weighted sums of complex Gaußian distributions with the PIK approach is central to this application. In a first step, PIKs map a real normal distribution to such a weighted sum, and this procedure is called the PIKfan. The PIKfan has the sampling cost of a real normal distribution. In a second step, this weighted sum is evolved with a second PIK into the distribution of the theory at hand. In combination, we reduce the sampling task for a general class of complex systems to a Gaußian one, and the main computational task is that of computing the PIK. We illustrate the approach with the one-site Hubbard model at arbitrary chemical potential and with $φ^4$-deformed extensions of it.

☆ Lattice-geometry dependence of Type-I and Type-II magnetic flux responses in strongly correlated bosons
Takayuki Yokoyama, Yasuhiro Tada
Superfluids and superconductors are classified into Type-I and Type-II according to their response to a magnetic flux, but this classification has hardly been addressed for lattice bosons under magnetic flux, where the Meissner and vortex phases have been studied mostly in ladder geometries. Here, we study the flux response of the extended Bose-Hubbard model with nearest-neighbor interaction $V$ at half filling on square and triangular ladders with two to four legs by using the density-matrix renormalization group. On the square ladders, the vortex phase is confined to a region near $V=0$. At finite $V$, a magnetic flux-induced charge-density-wave (CDW) order replaces it, and the response becomes Type-I-like. In contrast, on the triangular ladders, the vortex phase persists over the whole range of $V$ studied, and the response remains Type-II-like. By extrapolating the ladder results to two dimensions, we argue that the Type-I or Type-II character of the flux response depends on the lattice geometry, which suggests a role of geometric frustration.

☆ Comparing weakly interacting and free quantum dynamics locally
Jorge Acuña Flores, Joscha Henheik, Marius Lemm, Daniele Toniolo
Lieb-Robinson bounds (LRBs) have become a standard tool for perturbative results in quantum many-body physics, including gap stability and many-body adiabatic theory. Here, we use LRBs to locally approximate weakly interacting many-body dynamics with one-body dynamics on large, perturbative time scales. This allows us to use one-body transport results to establish the expected many-body transport behavior on finite time scales in the following two illustrative settings: (i) We prove quantum diffusion, as quantified by a certain operator spreading diagnostic, in weakly interacting and weakly disordered Fermi systems in dimensions $D\geq2$ on large finite time scales based on the non-interacting diffusion result of Black, Drogin, and Hernández [arXiv:2506.06468]. (ii) We show for Fermi-Hubbard models with initially low spin-down density, that all local multi-time spin-up correlation functions are approximated by their free counterparts. In particular, we obtain an OTOC (out-of-time-ordered correlator) counterpart to the patterns of short-time entanglement related to lattice path counts observed numerically by Bippus et al. [Phys. Rev. B 113, 035152 (2026)].

☆ Quantum computing for gearing down complex many-fermion problems
Weijie Du, Filippo Fornetti, James P. Vary
Quantum computing unlocks exciting opportunities to extend first-principles calculations of quantum many-body systems beyond classical computing limits. Despite advances in algorithms and proof-of-principle experiments, large-scale {\it ab initio} calculations on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices remain challenging. We introduce a quantum-classical framework that identifies compact single-particle bases to bring otherwise intractable many-fermion problems within classical reach while preserving an accurate ground-state description. We develop an efficient adaptive search scheme driven by simulated annealing that jointly optimizes natural-orbital-guided transformations and active-space selections. A quantum-assisted ground-state estimator provides search guidance using low-depth circuits and relaxed accuracy requirements, making the framework promising for NISQ devices. We demonstrate the framework's applicability for the nuclear structure of the oxygen isotopes. Our framework opens a new route to tackling complex {\it ab initio} many-fermion problems across disciplines through quantum-assisted basis reduction.

☆ Pairing and modular: Generalized electrons and quasiholes inside the $\boxtimes$ of topological orders
Yoshiki Fukusumi, Yuma Furuta
We study the relationship between the pair creation mechanism in physics and the pairing ($\boxtimes_{\mathbf{A}_{\text{ub}}}$) in mathematics, focusing on the modular and algebraic properties. We provide a way to couple two topologically ordered systems, $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{A'}$ sharing the common (non-group-like) structure $\mathbf{A}_{\text{ub}}=\overline{\mathbf{A'}_{\text{ub}}}$, through the nonabelian anyon analog of the pair creation mechanism denoted as $\mathbf{A}_{\text{ub},\boxtimes}=\mathbf{A}_{\text{ub}}\boxtimes \mathbf{A'}_{\text{ub}}$. We identify $\mathbf{A}_{\text{ub},\boxtimes}$ as the generalized version of electron operators in general topological orders or hidden current with (half-)integer spin involving the conformal embeddings. We provide a way to construct $\mathbf{A}_{\text{ub},\boxtimes}$ as the hidden topological operator and identify $\mathbf{A}\boxtimes_{\mathbf{A}_{\text{ub}}}\mathbf{A'}$, a general class of topoloical orders, as the $\mathbf{A}_{\text{ub},\boxtimes}$-extended symmetry topological field theory. We also conjecture a series of underlying (unexplored) modular invariants, connecting the conformal embedding and the pairing.

☆ Role of antisite disorder in dictating the Ising anisotropy and ferromagnetic ground state of NdGaSi
Anyesh Saraswati, Sourav Kanthal, Subhajit Nandy, Jhuma Sannigrahi, Matthias Gutmann, Nitesh Kumar
Single-ion anisotropy and exchange interactions together set the magnetic ground state of rare-earth intermetallics, yet the role of chemical disorder on the ligand sublattice remains little explored. Here, we show that Ga/Si antisite disorder in NdGaSi stabilises the centrosymmetric $I4_1/amd$ structure and raises the Nd$^{3+}$ site symmetry to $D_{2d}$, which forbids all $m=\pm2$ Stevens operators in the crystalline electric field (CEF) Hamiltonian. Magnetization, specific heat, single-crystal neutron diffraction, and x-ray absorption spectroscopy establish the disordered structure and a collinear ferromagnetic order below $T_\mathrm{C}\approx11$~K with Ising anisotropy along $c$. A CEF analysis that fits the susceptibilities along both axes and the magnetic specific heat simultaneously yields a ground-state doublet that is $\sim97\%$ pure, in contrast to the strongly mixed ground state of the Al/Si-ordered NdAlSi ($C_{2v}$ site symmetry of Nd$^{3+}$). We argue that this ground-state purity makes the ordered moment rigid against the modulation due to frustrated exchange, selecting a $\mathbf{k}=0$ ferromagnet in NdGaSi instead of the incommensurate ferrimagnet of NdAlSi. Antisite disorder, thus, acts as a handle on CEF ground-state purity and can, thereby, select between fundamentally different magnetic ground states.

☆ Nonmonotonic Magnetic Correlations in Decorated Lieb-Lattice Anderson Models
Raymond Hmuifoo, Edwin W. Huang, Annabelle Ancheta, Richard T. Scalettar
The interplay between electronic correlations and lattice geometry can strongly modify the competition between magnetic correlations and local singlet formation in multiorbital Hamiltonians. Here we use determinant quantum Monte Carlo simulations to investigate two periodic Anderson-like models constructed by selectively hybridizing localized orbitals to the inequivalent sites of a Lieb lattice. The resulting geometries possess partially filled flat bands and different sublattice imbalances. We examine the evolution of local spin correlations and orbital-resolved magnetic structure factors as the hybridization is increased. Although correlations between hybridized orbitals evolve relatively smoothly toward local singlet formation, the longer-range magnetic correlations exhibit a striking nonmonotonic dependence on hybridization. In particular, we observe a pronounced suppression at intermediate hybridization followed by a substantial recovery on undecorated lattice sites. We discuss these results in relation to earlier studies of depleted periodic Anderson models and the constraints imposed by Lieb's theorem. Our findings illustrate how selective hybridization and flat-band structure can produce unusual redistributions of magnetic correlations in strongly interacting multiorbital systems.

☆ Kinetic Arrest of a Disordered First-Order Phase Transition in Strained V2O3 Thin Films
Sindhunil Barman Roy
We develop a continuum phenomenological theory for the kinetic arrest (KA) of a first-order phase transition (FOPT), taking the thermal and electric field-driven metal-insulator transition (MIT) in epitaxial V2O3 thin films as a prototype. By defining a coarse-grained mesoscopic order parameter representing the metallic volume fraction coupled to the primary structural monoclinic distortion, we formulate a Time-Dependent Ginzburg-Landau (TDGL) framework integrated with a non-local elastic interaction kernel and an Imry-Wortis quenched disorder landscape. We derive an explicit dynamic criterion for the kinetic arrest boundary TK(E) by analyzing the divergence of the intrinsic order-parameter relaxation time relative to experimental observation timescales. Our framework rigorously decouples the thermodynamic driving force from the kinetic activation barrier. We demonstrate that epitaxial substrate-induced clamping elevates local elastic barriers, pinning domain boundaries and stabilizing an arrested, inhomogeneous mosaic of metallic and insulating phases down to cryogenic temperatures. The simulated transformation kinetics exhibit an Avrami exponent suppression to values n < 1, reflecting slow, hindered domain-wall propagation. Furthermore, we examine the effect of an external electric field as an isothermal mechanism that lowers this kinetic barrier, providing a phenomenological description of threshold de-arrest and multi-level resistance states. We critically discuss this electronic barrier-lowering mechanism in comparison with electrothermal Joule heating, establish diagnostic criteria to distinguish them, and contextualize these non-equilibrium dynamics with related phenomena in disordered superconducting films.

☆ Quantum order by disorder among lozenge tilings: a staircase of hub-free crystals between the Lieb ferrimagnet and the antiferromagnet
Suhwan Yoo, Jeehoon Choi, Chaeyeon Kim, Hee Young Kwon, Changyeon Won
Lozenge tilings of the triangular lattice define an exponentially large family of bipartite networks, from the dice lattice, a Lieb ferrimagnet with the largest sublattice imbalance, to square-type tilings, which are compensated antiferromagnets. For the classical Heisenberg antiferromagnet all of them are degenerate. We show that quantum fluctuations lift this degeneracy through a local mechanism: the zero-point energy is, to leading order, a sum of site terms that are convex in the coordination $z$, so that Jensen's inequality at fixed $\langle z\rangle=4$ selects the square-type tiling. An expansion about the Ising limit explains the convexity: a site with more bonds has more channels for quantum fluctuations, but each fluctuation frustrates more bonds. A magnetic field couples to the Lieb moment and competes with this selection. Because the moment is carried most cheaply by threefold and fivefold sites, sixfold hubs are avoided, and bond counting together with the Lieb--Mattis theorem limits hub-free tilings to $3/5$ of the dice moment. Quantum Monte Carlo and a complete enumeration of periodic tilings with small unit cells show that the classical jump is replaced by a staircase of periodic crystals. Its widest step is a hub-free crystal that saturates the bound; below it, threefold and fivefold defects pack ever more densely in a shallow sequence of crystals, controlled by a short-ranged attraction between defects of equal curvature and a repulsion between defects of opposite curvature. Selection energies scale as $JS$. In the height representation the coordination is the discrete Gaussian curvature and the Lieb moment its sublattice-staggered part. We give spectroscopic signatures and discuss realizations in nanographenes, atomic spin arrays and quantum simulators.
☆ Growth and anisotropic directional dependent transport properties of Altermagnetic CrSb
Resham Babu Regmi, Hari Bhandari, Sk Jamaluddin, Abhijeet Nayak, Ashok Chaudhary, Mohamed El Gazzah, Alex T. Sheardy, Maksym Zhukovskyi, Allen G. Oliver, Nirmal J. Ghimire
CrSb is a metallic altermagnet exhibiting large momentum-dependent spin splitting and antifer- romagnetic ordering well above room temperature. Although its electronic and magnetotransport properties have attracted considerable attention, a systematic comparison of crystals prepared us- ing different growth methods remains limited. Here we investigate the structural, magnetic, and anisotropic transport properties of CrSb single crystals grown by Sb(self)-flux, Bi flux, and chem- ical vapor transport (CVT). Each of these growth reveals distinct crystal morphologies. Magne- tization measurements exhibit broadly consistent antiferromagnetic responses, with an additional low-temperature contribution observed in Bi-flux-grown crystals. All samples display metallic resis- tivity and positive, nonsaturating magnetoresistance up to 9 T. Sb-flux- and CVT-grown crystals exhibit comparable residual resistivity ratios and magnetoresistance, whereas Bi-flux-grown crys- tals show enhanced residual resistivity and a substantially reduced magnetoresistance, consistent with stronger carrier scattering. Hall measurements reveal a pronounced dependence on the field- current configuration, including nonlinear field dependence and opposite Hall polarities for different crystallographic orientations. These results establish the reproducibility of anisotropic magneto- transport across distinct growth routes while highlighting the sensitivity of carrier scattering to crystal-growth conditions. Our findings provide a comparative framework for selecting CrSb single crystals for orientation-dependent transport and spintronic investigations.

☆ Energy and Charge Transmission at Conformal Interfaces: Relations and Bounds
Yuma Furuta, Yuya Kusuki, Toshiki Onagi, Yin Tang
Symmetry constrains how independently energy and charge can pass through a conformal interface. For interfaces between Wess--Zumino--Witten (WZW) models $G_{k_L}$ and $G_{k_R}$ preserving the diagonal affine algebra, we derive an exact relation between the energy and charge transmission coefficients, $c_{LR}=2(\dim G)k_{LR}/(k_L+k_R+2h^\vee)$. Together with positivity of outgoing energy, this relation excludes complete energy transmission at unequal levels. With additional bulk degrees of freedom, the equality is replaced by bounds controlled by the coset central charges. Complete transmission from a lower-level WZW model then imposes a lower bound on the coset central charge on the other side. In linear response, the relation fixes the ratio of thermal to charge conductance to the harmonic mean of the two bulk ratios, independently of the interface, while coset sectors bound the thermal conductance at fixed charge conductance. This interface-independent ratio is a generalized Wiedemann--Franz law for conformal interfaces between WZW models. The charge transmission coefficient $k_{LR}$ also governs equilibrium charge fluctuations and fixes the leading quadratic dependence of the boundary-condition-changing operator's scaling dimension on the rotation angle.

☆ Intertwined Magneto-Structural Criticality Driving Heterogeneous Collective-Pseudospin Dynamics in Sr2IrO4
Arnab Singh, Junyoung Kwon, AM Milinda Abeykoon
Correlated quantum phenomena arising from spin-orbit-coupled degrees of freedom provide foundational paradigms in emerging quantum technologies and spin-based functionalities. Elucidating the cooperative behaviors of these systems requires a precise probing of their intertwined magnetic and structural configurations. Using complementary resonant X-ray diffraction and high-energy total scattering measurements on single crystals of Sr2IrO4, we observe that spontaneous structural distortions scale quadratically with the magnetic order parameter. Importantly, the lattice distortion inherits the characteristic 2D XY -like critical behavior of the underlying antiferromagnetic order. X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS) reveals multiscale, temperature- and wave-vector-dependent magnetic dynamics characterized by compressed-exponential relaxation and signatures of critical slowing down near the magnetic transition. These findings suggest the role of spin-orbit coupling and local structural distortions as the possible mechanism orchestrating such unconventional dynamics.

Guan-Lin Lin, Xiaodong Hu, Di Xiao, Ying Ran
We study a phase transition between a superfluid phase and a fractional Chern insulator phase in a hard-core boson model on the honeycomb lattice using symmetric hyperdeterminant (Hdet) wavefunctions. Combining projective symmetry group analysis with variational Monte Carlo, we construct and optimize Hdet states in various symmetry classes. Based on the associated effective theories, we show that different symmetry classes, i.e., representations of the projective symmetry group, describe specific quantum phases. Compared with traditional fermionic parton construction, the symmetric Hdet wavefunctions are shown to improve microscopics significantly, allowing quantitative investigation of quantum phase diagrams. We argue that, in contrast with the common belief, this putative continuous phase transition is described by a fluctuating $SU(2)_g$ gauge field coupling with four Dirac nodes forming two $SU(2)_g$ doublets (i.e., $N_f=2$ QCD).

☆ State-selective dynamical freezing in driven Rydberg atom chains
Madhumita Sarkar, Sougato Bose, Roopayan Ghosh
Dynamical freezing, the near-complete suppression of dynamics at special drive frequencies, offers a route to mitigating Floquet heating in periodically driven quantum systems. In interacting systems, however, the energy cost of each transition depends on the many-body configuration, so that the freezing condition itself becomes state dependent. We study this dependence in periodically driven Rydberg atom chains under single- and bi-frequency driving. Using Floquet perturbation theory, we show that each spin flip is characterised by a single interference amplitude set by its local interaction shift, and that a state freezes only where the amplitudes of all its available flips vanish simultaneously. This picture accounts quantitatively for the shift and proliferation of freezing frequencies with interatomic spacing and for the response of entire families of initial states, which are sorted by a single local motif. Freezing is strong only within a window of spacings bounded by interaction tails on one side and nearest-neighbour excitation facilitation on the other, outside of which the advantage of bi-frequency driving is lost. In the regime of large detuning amplitude, where freezing points are numerous and the perturbative description is controlled, this window leaves almost no room for the PXP limit.

♻ ☆ Max-Cut on Token Graphs
José Angel Alejandro-Soto, Paulo T. Araujo, Ruy Fabila-Monroy, Sergio Gerardo Gómez-Galicia, Mohamed Hibat-Allah, Md Moshiur Rahman Raj, Mahmud Ashraf Shamim, Ana Laura Trujillo-Negrete
Let $G$ be a graph on $n$ vertices, with a positive weight assigned to each edge. A cut of $G$ is a partition of its vertices into two sets $X$ and $Y$; the weight of $(X,Y)$ is the sum of the weight of the edges of $G$ with one endpoint in $X$ and the other endpoint in $Y$. The Max-Cut problem asks for the maximum weight, $m(G)$, of a cut of $G$. The $k$-token graph of $G$, is the graph, $F_k(G)$, whose vertices are the $k$-subsets of vertices of $G$, two of them being adjacent when their symmetric difference is an edge of $G$. The phase-reconstruction problem for Heisenberg antiferromagnets in physics can be rephrased as a Max-Cut problem on token graphs. Motivated by this, we study the Max-Cut problem on token graphs, mainly when all edges are assigned the same weight. Our main focus is to bound $m(F_k(G))$ in terms of $m(G)$. We prove that $m(F_k(G))\geq\binom{n-2}{k-1}m(G)$, and that this bound is tight up to a multiplicative factor of $1+O(k/n)$; in the case when $k=c \cdot n$ for some constant $0 < c < 1$, we provide an example where this bound is off by a multiplicative constant factor. We also show bounds for $m(F_k(G))$ for various classes of graphs $G$. Finally, we consider the algorithmic complexity of finding $m(F_k(G))$, showing it to be NP-complete for a constant $k$, and giving evidence that, when the weights take finitely many values, it is not NP-hard for $k\geq n^δ$ for any constant $δ>0$.

By extracting the local dynamic susceptibility from INS spectra and applying the total moment sum rule, we find that both undoped and Li-doped $α$-MnTe exhibit a nearly full expected Mn$^{2+}$ local moment of $\approx5.9~μ_\mathrm{B}$ with $S=5/2$. ♻ ☆ Non-Equilibrium Instantaneous Approximation and Dipole Forbidden d-d Transitions
Marco Marino, Lasse Sternemann, Mirko Cinchetti, Frithjof B. Anders
Time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy provides direct access to pump-induced changes in the electronic structure of correlated materials, but its theoretical description generally requires computationally demanding two-time non-equilibrium calculations. We introduce an instantaneous approximation for pump-driven correlated systems, based on a separation between the rapid decay of the Green's functions in the relative time variable and their slower evolution in the average time. Combined with a one-shot dynamical mean-field construction at the Hubbard I level, the method incorporates the driven dynamics of the local correlated shell into the lattice Green's function while retaining momentum resolution. We also derive an effective coupling for nominally dipole-forbidden d-d excitations. It arises from a dipole-allowed d-p transition followed by p-d hybridization; beyond the instantaneous limit, the same process produces an energy-dependent vertex correction to the optical response. As a proof of principle, we apply the framework to paramagnetic and antiferromagnetic FePS3, using a density-functional theory derived tight-binding model together with a supercell unfolding procedure. The calculated momentum-resolved spectra reproduce the main qualitative features observed after excitation of the first and second d-d transitions in recent time-resolved photoemission experiments.

Theo N. Dionne, Maia G. Vergniory
Can crystalline symmetry reveal where charge localizes in a strongly correlated insulator? We show that occupied symmetry-resolved spectral weights of the exact electronic Green's function define effective atomic limits. In an interacting Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain, their displacement tracks the spin-resolved many-body polarization across distinct insulating phases. A quantum metric of the one-body reduced density matrix provides a complementary geometric characterization. Our results extend real-space symmetry analysis beyond occupied-band projectors.
♻ ☆ Lowering the temperature of two-dimensional fermionic tensor networks with cluster expansions
Sander De Meyer, Atsushi Ueda, Yuchi He, Nick Bultinck, Jutho Haegeman
Representing the time-evolution operator as a tensor network constitutes a key ingredient in several algorithms for studying quantum lattice systems at finite temperature or in a non-equilibrium setting. For a Hamiltonian composed of strictly short-ranged interactions, the Suzuki-Trotter decomposition is the main technique for obtaining such a representation. In [B.~Vanhecke, L.~Vanderstraeten and F.~Verstraete, Physical Review A, L020402 (2021)], an alternative strategy, the cluster expansion, was introduced. We extend the cluster expansion to two-dimensional fermionic systems, and employ it to construct projected entangled-pair operator (PEPO) approximations of Gibbs states. We also discuss and benchmark different truncation schemes for multiplying layers of PEPOs together.
